title: SYSK Selects: What Happened at Kent State?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on the Kent State shootings of May 4, 1970. Josh introduces it as a pick. The hosts trace the roots in Vietnam, Nixon's April 1970 invasion of Cambodia, and the campus protests of May 1 to May 4, including the burning of the ROTC building, Mayor Satrom's bar closure, Governor Rhodes's inflammatory press conference, the guard's confrontation on Blanket Hill, and the shooting that killed four students and wounded nine. They cover Glenn Frank's role in calming the crowd, the official responses from Nixon and Agnew, the presidential commission and FBI findings, the trials and small civil settlement, the Ohio National Guard's expression of regret, the university's memorialization efforts, and later audio evidence. They also discuss the Jackson State shootings ten days later, in which two Black students were killed. The episode ends with listener mail from a former prison guard responding to an earlier capital punishment episode.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a Selects pick on the Kent State massacre. Chuck and Josh chat about snow and the Neil Young song Ohio, which Chuck has not heard.

segments.title: Background: Vietnam and Nixon's Cambodia invasion
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Vietnam War's origins after the French departure, US containment policy, Nixon's Vietnamization promise, and his April 30, 1970 announcement of the invasion of Cambodia, which sparked protests.

segments.title: Kent State protests, May 1 and the weekend of bonfires
segments.summary: Kent State students held an anti-war protest on May 1 and the hosts describe the Friday protest where the Constitution was buried. That night drinking led to bonfires, bottles thrown at police cars, and Mayor Leroy Satrom closing the bars, prompting police tear gas.

segments.title: Saturday ROTC fire and Governor Rhodes's press conference
segments.summary: On Saturday about a thousand protesters burned the ROTC building, and cut fire hoses. The National Guard arrived. On Sunday Governor James Rhodes held a press conference calling protesters the worst type of people and mentioning martial law, which the guard took as a declaration.

segments.title: Monday rally and General Canterbury's bullhorn
segments.summary: On Monday, with martial law flyers circulating and a ban on assemblies in effect, about three thousand people gathered and some hundreds protested. General Canterbury tried to disperse the crowd by bullhorn from a jeep, and protesters threw rocks. Guardsmen loaded weapons.

segments.title: The shooting on Blanket Hill
segments.summary: Guardsmen pushed the crowd over Blanket Hill toward Prentice Hall, were cornered by a fence, and retreated up the hill. At the top, some turned and fired about 61 to 67 shots in roughly thirteen seconds. Four students were killed, including Sandra Scheuer and William Schroeder who were walking to class, and nine were wounded.
topics: Allison Krause Jeffrey Miller Sandra Scheuer William Schroeder

segments.title: Glenn Frank's role and the strike
segments.summary: Faculty marshal Glenn Frank and his team stepped between the guardsmen and students, got the guard to stop firing, and calmed the students, likely preventing further violence. The university closed for the semester, and a hundred thousand people went to Washington the following weekend.

segments.title: Aftermath, official responses, investigations, and trials
segments.summary: Nixon called dissent turning to violence an invitation to tragedy, and Agnew called the students scared kids with guns. Guardsmen claimed a sniper and self-defense, later disputed. The presidential commission called the shooting unnecessary, unwarranted, and inexcusable, and an FBI probe found the defense fabricated. A poll blamed protesters, a federal case was dismissed, and a 1979 civil settlement paid a small sum to the families. The Guard issued a statement of regret, and the university's memorial efforts and visitors center are discussed.

segments.title: Audio evidence, shots before the volley, and Jackson State
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a recording with the words get, set, point, fire, and analysis suggesting shots before the guard fired, with student photographer Terry Norman accused. They then cover the Jackson State shootings ten days later in Mississippi, where police fired into a dormitory, killing two Black students, James Green and Philip Gibbs.

segments.title: Listener mail: prison guards
segments.summary: A listener who was a former prison guard responds to the hosts' earlier capital punishment episode, saying guards are portrayed too negatively and describing inmate razor rights on death row.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: The hosts suggest searching for Kent State and Jackson State on the website and sign off with contact information.
